ren-2.title: Renal physiology 2: Physiology of the nephron

P1.A: Yes: urea, uric acid and creatinine are removed.
P1.B: Yes: the kidneys clear hormones from the blood.
P1.C: Yes: toxic substances are among the exogenous chemicals removed.
P1.D: Yes: therapeutic medications are exogenous chemicals the kidneys remove.
P1.E: No: blood cells are too big to pass the filter; red cells in urine are abnormal (hematuria).

P2.A: Yes: urea, made by the liver from ammonia, is the main nitrogenous waste.
P2.B: No: glucose in urine (glucosuria) is abnormal; all filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed.
P2.C: Yes: creatinine, from creatine phosphate breakdown, is a normal waste.
P2.D: Yes: uric acid, from nucleic acid breakdown, is a normal waste.
P2.E: Yes: the kidneys regulate electrolytes, so sodium is normally excreted.

P3.A: Abnormal: albumin in urine is albuminuria.
P3.B: Abnormal: glucose in urine is glucosuria.
P3.C: Normal: sodium is an electrolyte the kidneys excrete every day.
P3.D: Abnormal: red cells in urine is hematuria.
P3.E: Normal: potassium is an electrolyte the kidneys excrete every day.

P4.A: Yes: osmolarity is on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.B: Yes: blood volume and pressure are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.C: No: calcitriol synthesis is listed under general (whole-body) homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.
P4.D: Yes: electrolyte concentrations are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.E: No: gluconeogenesis in starvation is listed under general homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.

P46.A: No: gluconeogenesis is listed under general (whole-body) homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.
P46.B: Yes: blood volume and pressure are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P46.C: Yes: electrolyte concentrations are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P46.D: Yes: blood volume is on the slide for blood homeostasis.

P47.A: Yes: toxic substances are among the exogenous chemicals removed.
P47.B: Yes: urea, uric acid and creatinine are removed.
P47.C: No: blood cells are not filtered; red cells in urine are abnormal.
P47.D: Yes: the kidneys clear hormones from the blood.

P48.A: No: glucose is filtered but all of it is normally reabsorbed; in urine it is abnormal.
P48.B: Yes: uric acid, from nucleic acid breakdown, is a waste the kidneys remove.
P48.C: Yes: creatinine, from creatine phosphate breakdown, is a waste the kidneys remove.
P48.D: No: albumin is held back by the negatively charged filter; in urine it is abnormal.

P49.A: Yes: the kidneys regulate blood volume and pressure.
P49.B: Yes: they regulate acid-base balance (H+ and HCO3-).
P49.D: No: PaCO2 is set by breathing, the lungs, not the kidneys.

P5.A: Yes: GFR is about 2 mL per second, 120 mL per minute.
P5.B: Yes: about 170 L a day, which is the body fluids filtered about 4 times a day.
P5.C: Yes: of 120 mL/min filtered, 119 are reabsorbed and about 1 mL becomes urine.
P5.D: No: ADH reduces urine by increasing water reabsorption in the collecting duct, not by lowering filtration.
P5.E: Yes: molecules under 3 nm (glucose, nitrogenous wastes) pass freely through the filter.

P6.A: Yes: glucose is small (under 3 nm) and passes the filter freely.
P6.B: Yes: normally all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.
P6.C: Yes: glucose is co-transported with Na+ by SGLT proteins.
P6.D: Yes: basal Na+–K+ pumps push Na+ out so it does not build up in the cells.
P6.E: No: glucosuria comes when blood glucose is too high and the carriers are saturated, not when it is low.

P7.A: Yes: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary.
P7.C: No: ADH does not act on filtration.
P7.D: Yes: it inserts aquaporins so more water is reabsorbed.
P7.E: No: ADH acts on the collecting duct, not the proximal tubule.

P8.A: Yes: renin starts the chain to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor.
P8.B: No: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation, so they lower pressure.
P8.C: Yes: aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na+ and water, raising plasma volume.
P8.D: No: diuretics increase urine and lower plasma volume.
P8.E: Yes: ADH increases water reabsorption and constricts vessels.

P9.A: Yes: ACE inhibitors stop angiotensin II, so vessels dilate and less aldosterone is made.
P9.B: No: renin leads to angiotensin II, a vasoconstrictor.
P9.C: No: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor.
P9.D: No: ADH increases water reabsorption and plasma volume.
P9.E: Yes: ANP dilates vessels and makes the kidneys lose Na+ and water.

P10.A: Yes: renin leads to angiotensin II and aldosterone.
P10.B: No: inulin is a marker used to measure GFR; it has no effect on pressure.
P10.C: Yes: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor raising blood pressure.
P10.D: Yes: aldosterone raises Na+ and water reabsorption, so volume and pressure rise.
P10.E: Yes: ADH raises water reabsorption and constricts vessels.
